Review of Last Class

The Grid Is a Choice We Make

The plume equation gives a concentration at every point. A grid is how we look at it, and looking is not free.

Monday: the samples themselves are exact, but everything we compute from them — a maximum, a location, an area — depends on where the samples fell.

Sigma Sets the Spacing

\(\sigma_y\) grows from a couple of metres near the stack to hundreds of metres downwind.

A grid that resolves the plume far away can step straight over it near the source.

Superposition Creates New Structure

Three stacks that each comply can jointly violate, and the combined maximum sits where no single plume peaks.

What Are We Even Claiming?

A Model Gave You a Number

You have simulated a sag curve, a footprint, a capacity plan.

A regulator asks: why should I believe this?

“I solved the equations correctly” answers a different question than the one being asked.

Where Did Every Parameter Come From?

Every model we have built this term needed numbers. We have never asked where they came from.

Model Parameters Where they came from
Shallow lake \(b\), \(q\), \(m\) Literature values for a lake type
Airshed box \(u\), \(k\), \(S\) Given in the problem statement
Streeter-Phelps \(k_a\), \(k_c\), \(k_n\) Fitted to measurements
Gaussian plume \(\sigma_y\), \(\sigma_z\) Table lookup by stability class

Only one of those rows involves data from the system being modeled.

Three Ways to Be Wrong

  1. Numerical: the equations are right, the grid or step size is too coarse.
  2. Parametric: the structure is right, the parameter values are wrong.
  3. Structural: the model is the wrong model for this system.

You Already Fixed the First One

Numerical error is the friendly kind: you control it, and you can drive it toward zero.

Halve the step, watch the answer stop moving, report what changed. Week 4 in time, Monday in space.

No amount of refinement fixes the other two.

Today: The Other Two

Parametric error has a standard treatment — calibration — and a standard trap.

Structural error has neither.

Calibration: Fitting to Data

Calibrating the DO Model

\(k_a\), \(k_c\), and \(k_n\) are not constants of nature. They depend on the river: its turbulence, its temperature, what is actually in the waste.

In practice you measure dissolved oxygen downstream and fit the rates to it.

The Data We Would Actually Have

Code 
# Seeded so the lecture reports the same numbers every time it renders.
Random.seed!(3)

observation_step = 8                      # one observation every 2 km on a 0.25 km grid
truth = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, true_params)
observation_index = 1:observation_step:length(truth)
observation_distance = [(i - 1) * Δx for i in observation_index]
observations = truth[observation_index] + rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index))

p_data = scatter(observation_distance, observations, color=cb_vermillion, markersize=7,
    xlabel="Distance downstream  [km]", ylabel="DO  [mg/L]",
    label="measurements", legend=:bottomright)
plot!(p_data, 0:Δx:river_length, truth, color=:black, linewidth=4, label="model that generated them")
plot!(p_data, size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

Score Two Candidates By Hand

Pick the parameters that make the simulation closest to the measurements:

\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y^\text{sim}_i - y^\text{obs}_i\right)^2}\]

Code 
rmse(simulated, observed) = sqrt(mean((simulated .- observed).^2))

function do_rmse(ka, kc, kn)
    candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0,
                   Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U)
    simulated = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate)
    return rmse(simulated[observation_index], observations)
end

Before handing anything to a solver, score two guesses:

  • \((k_a, k_c, k_n) = (0.6, 0.4, 0.25)\), the true values: RMSE 0.179
  • \((k_a, k_c, k_n) = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)\), a naive start: RMSE 1.017

Handing It to a Solver

Code 
lower_bounds = [0.05, 0.05, 0.05]
upper_bounds = [2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
initial_guess = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]

calibration = Optim.optimize(v -> do_rmse(v[1], v[2], v[3]),
    lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess)
fitted = Optim.minimizer(calibration)

The Calibrated Fit

Code 
fitted_params = (; ka=fitted[1], kc=fitted[2], kn=fitted[3],
                   B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0,
                   Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U)

p_fit = scatter(observation_distance, observations, color=cb_vermillion, markersize=7,
    xlabel="Distance downstream  [km]", ylabel="DO  [mg/L]",
    label="measurements", legend=:bottomright)
plot!(p_fit, 0:Δx:river_length, truth, color=:black, linewidth=4, label="true model")
plot!(p_fit, 0:Δx:river_length, simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, fitted_params),
    color=cb_blue, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dash, label="calibrated model")
plot!(p_fit, size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

The Fit Is Not the Truth

We Recovered the Wrong Rates

Rate True Calibrated
\(k_a\) reaeration \(0.60\) 0.61
\(k_c\) CBOD decay \(0.40\) 0.35
\(k_n\) NBOD decay \(0.25\) 0.35

The calibration did not just miss. The two decay rates came back identical. The data cannot tell carbonaceous demand from nitrogenous demand, so the fit stopped distinguishing them.

It Fits Better Than the Truth

RMSE of the calibrated model: 0.1602 mg/L

RMSE of the true model: 0.1793 mg/L

This is not bad luck with one noise draw. Three free parameters chasing twenty-one noisy points will essentially always beat the truth in-sample.

Two Processes, One Curve

CBOD and NBOD both remove oxygen, and both decay exponentially downstream.

The measurements see only their sum. Faster carbonaceous decay and slower nitrogenous decay produce very nearly the same sag.

A Valley, Not a Basin

Code 
cbod_rates = 0.10:0.01:0.80
nbod_rates = 0.05:0.01:0.60
error_surface = [do_rmse(0.6, kc, kn) for kn in nbod_rates, kc in cbod_rates]

p_valley = contourf(cbod_rates, nbod_rates, error_surface, color=:viridis, linewidth=0,
    xlabel="CBOD decay rate  [1/d]", ylabel="NBOD decay rate  [1/d]")
scatter!(p_valley, [0.4], [0.25], color=:white, markersize=11, markershape=:star5,
    label="truth", legend=:topright)
scatter!(p_valley, [fitted[2]], [fitted[3]], color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9,
    label="calibrated")
plot!(p_valley, size=(1050, 470), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=10mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

Refit It Eight Times

Code 
# Score a candidate against any set of measurements, not just the ones above.
function rmse_against(ka, kc, kn, measured)
    candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0,
                   Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U)
    simulated = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate)
    return rmse(simulated[observation_index], measured)
end

# Nothing about the river changes across these refits. The only difference is
# which measurements we happened to take.
refit_ka = Float64[]
refit_kc = Float64[]
refit_kn = Float64[]

for seed in 1:8
    Random.seed!(seed)
    draw = truth[observation_index] + rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index))
    result = Optim.optimize(v -> rmse_against(v[1], v[2], v[3], draw),
        lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess)
    best = Optim.minimizer(result)
    push!(refit_ka, best[1])
    push!(refit_kc, best[2])
    push!(refit_kn, best[3])
end

The Same River, Eight Answers

Rate True Lowest Highest Spread
\(k_a\) reaeration \(0.60\) 0.58 0.61 0.03
\(k_c\) CBOD decay \(0.40\) 0.32 0.45 0.13
\(k_n\) NBOD decay \(0.25\) 0.2 0.35 0.15

Reaeration is pinned down. Nothing else pulls the curve back toward saturation, so the data can see it.

The two decay rates are not. They slide along the trough from one draw to the next, and on the draw we fitted earlier they landed on exactly the same value.

Nonuniqueness: the data constrain a combination of the rates, not the rates themselves. Which parameters a dataset can pin down, and which move together, is a question with real machinery behind it — here we are only meeting the symptom.

Controls

We Just Ran a Positive Control

We generated data from known parameters and asked whether the procedure could recover them.

That is a positive control: a test with a known right answer, run on the procedure rather than on the system.

What It Told Us

  • The procedure fits the data. It does not recover the parameters.
  • The failure is not a bug. It is a property of this model and this data.
  • We only know that because we knew the answer in advance.

The Other Control

A negative control feeds the procedure something with no signal in it and asks whether it finds one anyway.

If a calibration reports confident parameters when handed noise, its confident parameters mean nothing.

Fitting Pure Noise

Code 
# Same procedure, but the "measurements" are noise about a flat line ---
# there is no sag here for any parameter set to explain.
Random.seed!(11)
flat_observations = fill(mean(observations), length(observation_index)) +
    rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index))

function noise_rmse(ka, kc, kn)
    candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0,
                   Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U)
    rmse(simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate)[observation_index], flat_observations)
end

noise_fit = Optim.minimizer(Optim.optimize(v -> noise_rmse(v[1], v[2], v[3]),
    lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess))

It returns rates anyway: 0.41, 0.1, 0.19.

An optimiser always returns its argument minimum. Getting an answer is not evidence that there was one.

Validation: A Different Question

Calibration Is Not Validation

Following Oreskes et al. (1994):

  • Calibration: choosing parameters so simulations match observations.
  • Validation: establishing that the model is a legitimate basis for the claim you want to make.

Everything so far has been calibration. None of it was validation.

Two Kinds of Evidence

  • Empirical validity: does it predict data it has never seen? Hold observations back; do not fit them.
  • Face validity: are the processes in the model the ones that actually operate, parameterised the way they actually behave?

They fail independently. A model can predict well for the wrong reason, and be mechanistically right but useless.

A Plume From the Wrong Night

An engineer models a stack on a stable night — Class F. The night was actually Class E.

No parameter is being fitted here. The structure of the dispersion is wrong.

A Number Without a Diagnosis

RMSE across the twelve monitors: 567.3 µg/m³ — about 50% of the mean observed concentration.

The metric tells us how big the error is. It says nothing about what kind it is, and so nothing about whether calibration can fix it.

Can We Calibrate Our Way Out?

Wind speed is the obvious knob: genuinely uncertain, and the whole field scales as \(1/u\).

Code 
function wind_rmse(wind_speed)
    trial = (; emission=100.0, height=41.0, wind=wind_speed)
    modelled = [ground_concentration(monitor_downwind[i], monitor_crosswind[i],
        stability[:F], trial) for i in 1:length(monitor_downwind)]
    return rmse(modelled, monitor_observed)
end

wind_fit = Optim.optimize(v -> wind_rmse(first(v)), [0.3], [20.0], [2.5])
fitted_wind = first(Optim.minimizer(wind_fit))

Fitted wind: 2.53 m/s against a true \(2.5\). RMSE afterwards: 567.1 µg/m³, from 567.3.

The calibration returns a perfectly plausible wind speed and the error does not move.

The Residuals Say Otherwise

Code 
residual = monitor_modelled - monitor_observed

p_resid = scatter(monitor_downwind, residual, color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9,
    xlabel="Distance downwind  [km]", ylabel="Model − observed  [µg/m³]",
    legend=false)
hline!(p_resid, [0.0], color=:black, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash)
plot!(p_resid, size=(1100, 430), left_margin=14mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

A Shape Error, Not a Scale Error

Wind speed multiplies the whole field by a constant. It can lift the model or lower it — it cannot lift it near the stack and lower it far away.

The residuals change sign with distance. That is a plume spreading at the wrong rate, and no multiplicative parameter can absorb it. The optimiser was never going to find this.

A correct model with noisy data scatters its residuals around zero. RMSE squares them and averages — exactly the operation that throws the sign pattern away.

So What Would Have Caught It?

Calibrating the wind speed did not improve the RMSE, and would not have mattered if it had. The stability class would still be wrong.

  • Empirical check: plot residuals against every variable you have — distance, direction, time of day.
  • Face check: was it actually a stable night? Does the assumed class match the conditions?

Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

Key Takeaways

  • A model that fits better can be more wrong. Calibration minimises a metric, not error in the parameters.
  • Nonuniqueness is normal. Compensating processes mean data often constrain a combination of parameters.
  • An aggregate metric hides structure. Look at residuals, not just the scalar.
  • Controls test the procedure, not the system: positive asks whether it can recover a known answer, negative asks whether it invents one.
  • Empirical and face validity fail independently.

The Whole Arc, Once More

  • Forward Euler: error \(O(\Delta t)\) — halve the step, halve the error.
  • Monte Carlo: error \(O(n^{-1/2})\) — quadruple the samples, halve the error.
  • A grid on a closed form: the samples are exact; the error is in what you ask of them.
  • Calibration: the error does not shrink with effort at all. More optimisation makes the fit better and the parameters no more true.

Appendix

Why Compensating Processes Make a Valley

Both oxygen sinks decay exponentially in distance:

\[k_c B_0 e^{-k_c x/U} + k_n N_0 e^{-k_n x/U}\]

Over the stretch where measurements exist, raising \(k_c\) and lowering \(k_n\) leaves this sum nearly unchanged. The data constrain the sum; they do not separate the terms.

Reaeration is different in kind — it pulls toward \(C_s\) rather than away — so \(k_a\) stays identifiable.

The Lake, Revisited

Homework 3 asked what happens when a manager uses a one-stock lake model that ignores sediment recycling entirely.

That is structural error, met before we had a name for it: the fitted model is internally consistent and still sets an unsafe loading.
